title: Tenses
shortDescription: All twelve tense forms sorted by time and completeness, with signal words that instantly tell you which one a sentence wants.
genZNote: Twelve tenses sounds scary until you realise it's just 3 times times 4 aspects. English really said: tell me WHEN, or the sentence stays confusing.

sections.heading: The 3x4 framework
sections.body: English tense isn't twelve random forms to memorise separately — it's 3 TIMES (present, past, future) crossed with 4 ASPECTS (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Once you see the grid, you only need to learn what each of the 4 aspects DOES, and then apply that same logic to all three times.

sections.heading: What each aspect means (applies across all three times)

rows: A fact, habit, or single completed/future action
An action in progress at that time
An action completed before a reference point, with present relevance
An ongoing action that started earlier and continues up to a reference point
She has been writing since morning.
now, right now, at the moment, currently
already, yet, just, ever, since, for
while, when (interrupted action), at that time
before, after, by the time, already (in past context)
at this time tomorrow, this time next year
by the time, by next year

sections.heading: The confusions that decide most tense questions
bullets: Present Perfect vs Past Simple: use Present Perfect when the exact time isn't stated or the action connects to now ('I have finished my homework'); use Past Simple when a specific past time is given ('I finished my homework at 6 pm').
'Since' pairs with a POINT in time (since 2020, since Monday); 'for' pairs with a DURATION (for two years) — both usually go with a perfect tense, not simple past.
Past Perfect is used for the EARLIER of two past actions: 'The train had left BEFORE I reached the station' — had left happened first.
Never mix 'since' with simple past tense in the main clause — 'I am living here since 2015' is wrong; it must be 'I HAVE BEEN living here since 2015.'

sections.heading: A special exam trap: no future tense in time/conditional clauses
sections.body: In clauses starting with 'if', 'when', 'as soon as', 'before', 'after', 'until', English uses the PRESENT tense to talk about the future, even though the overall sentence is about a future event: 'I will call you WHEN I REACH home' (not 'will reach'). This is one of the most frequently tested tense-sequencing rules in competitive exams.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: English has 12 tense forms built from 3 times (present, past, future) crossed with 4 aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous), each triggered by specific signal words.
keyFacts: Present Perfect connects a past action to now; Past Simple states a finished action at a specific past time.
'Since' = a point in time; 'for' = a duration — both usually pair with a perfect tense.
Time/conditional clauses (if, when, before, until) use present tense even for future meaning.
commonConfusion: 'I am living here since 2015' is a very common but incorrect construction — it must be present perfect continuous.

highYieldFacts: 'I will call you when I reach home' — present tense in the time clause, even though the meaning is future.
Past Perfect marks the EARLIER of two past events; the later one stays in Past Simple.
commonTraps: Using 'will' inside an 'if/when' clause: 'If it will rain, we will cancel' should be 'If it rains...'
Pairing 'since' with simple past instead of a perfect tense.
Using Past Simple for both events in a two-past-event sentence instead of Past Perfect for the earlier one.
mustRemember: Signal words are the fastest way to identify the correct tense — train yourself to spot them first.

confusedTerms.distinction: Present Perfect is used when the exact time is unstated or the result matters now ('I have lost my keys'). Past Simple is used with a specific, finished past time ('I lost my keys yesterday').

possibleQuestions: Choose the correct form: 'By the time we arrived, the movie ___ (already start).'
Spot the error: 'I will let you know as soon as I will get the results.'
